creature.name: Khas-uu
creature.summary: Mongolian tiger spirit that guards southern forests, tests hunters, and serves as a symbol of royalty and authority

story.title: The Simurgh and the Burning Garden
story.summary: The great Simurgh descends from Mount Qaf to heal a garden scorched by divine fire, teaching a village the difference between destruction and renewal.

creature.name: Khodumodumo
creature.summary: A gargantuan swallowing monster from Basotho mythology that devours entire villages, defeated by a hero who cut his way out from within its stomach

story.title: The Peri and the Poet
story.summary: A grieving poet is visited by a Peri, a celestial spirit of Persian-Azerbaijani myth, who offers him a choice between forgetting his sorrow and learning its deeper meaning.

creature.name: Kibanda
creature.summary: Ugandan water spirit of Lake Bunyoro that controls fish abundance and rewards ethical fishermen with good catches

story.title: The Div and the Fortress of Fire
story.summary: A Div, a powerful demon of ancient Zoroastrian and Turkic tradition, builds a fortress of black stone to block the sun, and only a fearless blacksmith can challenge it.

creature.name: Kibati
creature.summary: Guinea-Bissau river dragon that brings prosperity or destruction depending on how communities treat the waters

story.title: The Bura of the Deep Waters
story.summary: Fishermen on the Kura River encounter a Bura, a water demon who demands a price for every fish pulled from the deep pools, and learn that some bargains are best left unmade.

creature.name: Kiev Ghost
creature.summary: Ukrainian ghost of a monk or soldier that haunts Kyiv streets at midnight, offering warnings and guidance to those in need

story.title: The Lungu of the Deep River
story.summary: A Bemba fisherman who overfishes a sacred river encounters the Lungu, a colossal serpent guardian who demands he restore what he has taken before the waters turn against the village.

creature.name: Kikimora
creature.summary: Kikimora is a female house spirit of dual nature — a domestic tutelary when the home is orderly, a malevolent tormentor when neglected

story.title: Kongamato of the Falls
story.summary: A Lozi hunter ventures too close to a hidden cataract above Victoria Falls and encounters the Kongamato, a pterodactyl-like beast that guards the spray zones where the living are not meant to wander.

creature.name: Kikimora
creature.summary: Kikimora is a female house spirit of dual nature — a domestic tutelary when the home is orderly, a malevolent tormentor when neglected

story.title: Funkwe the Devourer of Rivers
story.summary: When a Tonga village's river begins to vanish overnight, a young girl discovers that the Funkwe, a giant water serpent, has been drinking the river dry as punishment for the village chief's arrogance.

creature.name: Kikimora
creature.summary: Kikimora is a female house spirit of dual nature — a domestic tutelary when the home is orderly, a malevolent tormentor when neglected

story.title: Chitapo of the Silent Lake
story.summary: A woman grieving the loss of her child wanders to a lake in the Bangweulu wetlands and encounters Chitapo, a lake spirit who offers to return what was taken but demands a price measured in memory.

creature.name: Killer Whale
creature.summary: Haida supernatural whale spirit that rules the ocean, guides fishermen, and carries souls to the underwater spirit world

story.title: Nyaminyami and the Breaking of the Dam
story.summary: When engineers came to dam the Zambezi, the Tonga people warned that Nyaminyami, the river god, would not tolerate the severing of his body, and the floods that followed proved them right.

creature.name: Bukit Timah Monkey Man
creature.summary: Singapore's legendary cryptid said to inhabit Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, described as an upright-walking monkey-faced hominid

story.title: Glooscap and the Great Beaver: The Five Islands
story.summary: Glooscap once transformed himself into a giant beaver to create a safe haven for his people. Swimming in the Bay of Fundy, he slapped his enormous tail against the water with such tremendous force that it churned up the earth from the seabed, creating the Five Islands of Nova Scotia. When Glooscap slept, Nova Scotia was his bed and Prince Edward Island his pillow. In another tradition, when Glooscap finished painting all the splendor of the world, he dipped his brush into a blend of all the colors left over and created Abegweit, meaning Cradled on the Waves, his favorite island — Prince Edward Island. The Annapolis Valley was also shaped by Glooscap's hand. These landscape features are constant reminders to the Mi'kmaq of their culture hero's presence and his love for the land and its people.

creature.name: Bori (Iskoki)
creature.summary: Spirit beings from Hausa animism of Niger, created from hidden twin children, accessed through possession ceremonies

story.title: Oochigeas and the Invisible Boy (The Mi'kmaq Cinderella)
story.summary: A great chief had a son who was invisible. Only a woman who spoke the truth could see him. Many vain young women tried and failed, always lying that they could see the Invisible Boy. In a nearby village lived Oochigeas, the youngest daughter, whose face and hands were scarred from tending fires because her cruel elder sisters forced her to do all the hard work. Her ragged clothes were made of bark. She decided to try her luck and walked to the chief's lodge in tatters. The Invisible Boy's sister asked her the question: Can you see my brother? Oochigeas answered truthfully that she could not. Then the sister gave her fine clothes and combed her hair. Oochigeas approached again, and this time she saw the Invisible Boy — a handsome young man sitting at the edge of the sky. They married, and her kindness and truthfulness were rewarded, while her cruel sisters were punished.

creature.name: Baal
creature.summary: The Canaanite-Phoenician storm god who defeated the sea monster Yamm to establish cosmic order and shaped biblical Chaoskampf theology

story.title: Mooin, the Bear's Child
story.summary: A young Mi'kmaq boy wandered into the forest and became lost. A great she-bear found him and, instead of harming him, adopted him as her own cub. The boy grew up among the bear people, learning their ways and understanding the language of animals. He became strong and brave, but he always remembered that he was human. When he was grown, the bear people told him it was time to return to his own kind. Before he left, the bears taught him the songs and ceremonies they used to honor the Great Spirit, and gave him permission to hunt them for food — but only if he always showed respect and gratitude. The boy returned to the Mi'kmaq people as a great hunter and medicine man, teaching them the ceremony for honoring the spirits of the animals they killed. This is the origin of the Mi'kmaq hunting ceremonies and the Bear Clan tradition.

creature.name: Da (Aido-Hwedo)
creature.summary: The primordial rainbow serpent of Fon Vodun cosmology in Benin, who holds the world together and is worshipped as a cosmic support deity at the Python Temple of Ouidah

story.title: The Girl Chenoo
story.summary: A beautiful Mi'kmaq woman was lost in the frozen north and suffered terrible hunger. To survive, she ate human flesh and was transformed into a Chenoo — a cannibalistic ice monster with a heart of ice and an insatiable hunger for human beings. Her family searched for her but when they found her, she had become a monstrous giant with claws and fangs, her heart visible through her translucent chest. The family's oldest grandmother did not abandon her. She sang the old healing songs and performed the sacred ceremonies to warm her granddaughter's frozen heart. Through love and prayer, the grandmother melted the ice around the Chenoo's heart and restored her to human form. The story teaches the Mi'kmaq understanding that even those who become monsters through tragedy can be healed through family love, community, and the power of traditional ceremonies.

creature.name: Legba
creature.summary: The trickster gatekeeper deity of Fon Vodun in Benin, Legba controls communication between humans and spirits, standing at the crossroads of all worlds

story.title: Gluskabe and the Wind Eagle
story.summary: Gluskabe (Glooscap) was annoyed by the constant wind that made life difficult for his people. He traveled to the great mountain where the Wind Eagle — a colossal bird whose wingbeats created all the wind in the world — was perched. Gluskabe climbed the mountain and captured the Wind Eagle, tying its wings together so they could not move. Immediately the wind stopped. At first, everything was calm and pleasant, but soon the air grew hot and still. The water became stagnant, the people could not breathe, and the world began to suffocate. Gluskabe realized that the wind was necessary for life. He returned to the mountaintop and untied the Wind Eagle's wings — just a little — allowing a gentle breeze to flow. He learned that while too much wind is destructive, no wind at all is even worse. The Wind Eagle's wings have been tied ever since, which is why we have breezes but not constant gales.

creature.name: Agbé
creature.summary: The sea deity of Fon Vodun in Benin, Agbé rules the ocean, controls tides and marine life, and maintains cosmic balance between water and land

story.title: Tabaldak Creates Glooscap and Malsumis
story.summary: In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap and Malsumis. Glooscap was given the power to create a good world, full of kind animals, sweet fruits, and gentle rivers. Malsumis, the wolf, was his opposite, creating only evil — dangerous animals, thorns, and crooked rivers that flooded the land. From birth, Malsumis resented his brother and plotted to destroy him. Glooscap discovered that his brother could only be killed by a blow from a fern root. Malsumis tricked the animals into revealing this secret and attacked Glooscap, but the good twin was saved by Grandmother Woodchuck. Glooscap eventually defeated Malsumis and turned him into stone, where he remains, the embodiment of all that is harmful in nature.

creature.name: Kinkirsi (Kinkirga)
creature.summary: Nature spirits of the Mossi people of Burkina Faso, the Kinkirsi are invisible beings who inhabit wilderness spaces, participate in human procreation, and control wild animals

story.title: The Origin of Corn: First Mother's Sacrifice
story.summary: In the time of the first people, the Abenaki were hungry. Gluskabe's grandmother Nokomes taught the people to survive on wild plants, but food was scarce. First Mother, the first woman created by Gichi Niwaskw and Gluskabe, saw her children starving. She told her husband to kill her and drag her body across a clearing. Weeping, he obeyed. Where her body passed, corn sprang up — tall green stalks bearing golden ears. Where her heart lay, beans grew to climb the corn. Where her feet lay, squash spread across the ground. First Mother had given her life so her children would never starve. The Abenaki honor her sacrifice in every planting season, and the Three Sisters — corn, beans, and squash — are always planted together, as First Mother intended, supporting each other just as the people must support each other.

creature.name: Kintogou
creature.summary: A legendary guardian serpent from Mossi folklore of Burkina Faso that inhabits rivers and deep pools, controlling water and enforcing respect for natural water sources

story.title: Gluskonba and the Four Wishes
story.summary: Gluskonba (Glooscap) offered four Abenaki men a single wish each. The first man wished to be powerful and rich, and was turned into a great pine tree — tall and strong, but rooted in one place forever. The second man wished to be feared by everyone, and was turned into a bear — powerful but alone. The third man wished to live forever, and was turned into a rock — eternal but without feeling or movement. The fourth man listened to the fate of the others and asked only for the wisdom to accept whatever Gluskonba gave him. Gluskonba blessed this man with a long, happy life, many children, and the love of his community. The first three had received what they asked for, but found their wishes brought misery instead of happiness. The story teaches that true wisdom lies not in seeking power or wealth, but in accepting the gifts of the Creator with gratitude.

creature.name: Mba-Katrè
creature.summary: The hyena trickster figure in Mossi folklore of Burkina Faso, Mba-Katrè embodies gluttony and foolishness, consistently outwitted by the clever hare in moral education tales

story.title: Pamola, the Snow Bird Spirit of Mount Katahdin
story.summary: Pamola (also called Bemola or Pomola) is a powerful snow bird spirit who dwells on the summit of Mount Katahdin, the highest mountain in Maine and the most sacred peak of the Penobscot and Abenaki people. Pamola has the body of a man and the head and wings of a giant eagle and makes the cold weather by beating his enormous wings. He fiercely guards the mountain against trespassers, sending blizzards to drive away those who dare approach his domain. According to legend, a Penobscot woman once married Pamola and lived with him on the mountain, but she eventually grew homesick and returned to her village, bringing with her the knowledge of how to survive the mountain's winter. The Pamola legend serves as a warning to respect the sacred power of Mount Katahdin and the spirits that dwell there.

creature.name: Mba-Soêmba
creature.summary: The clever hare trickster of Mossi folklore in Burkina Faso, Mba-Soêmba consistently outwits larger animals through intelligence, teaching that wit triumphs over brute force

story.title: Gluskabe and Dzeedzeez (The Baby Who Outmatched the Hero)
story.summary: Gluskabe, the great culture hero, was resting in his lodge after his many labors when he heard a baby crying. The baby was Dzeedzeez (Wasis in Passamaquoddy), whose mother had left him alone while she gathered firewood. Gluskabe, confident in his powers, decided to quiet the baby himself. He tried using his magic, but the baby only cried louder. He sang his most powerful healing songs, but Dzeedzeez screamed. He tried every trick he knew — shapeshifting, illusions, promises of gifts — and Dzeedzeez simply stared at him and continued wailing. Finally, the great Gluskabe, who had defeated monsters and giants and even his evil twin brother, was utterly defeated by a baby. He left the lodge humbled, realizing that some challenges cannot be overcome by strength or magic. The story teaches that wisdom sometimes comes from recognizing one's own limitations.

creature.name: Sumbo
creature.summary: Sacred ritual masks of the Bwaba people of Burkina Faso that embody ancestral and bush spirits, central to the Do initiatory cult and community ceremonies

story.title: How Gluskabe Stole Tobacco
story.summary: In the early days, tobacco was guarded jealously by Grasshopper (or a giant), who kept it hidden from humanity. The people prayed for tobacco to use in their ceremonies, as it was the sacred plant that carried their prayers to the Creator. Gluskabe heard their pleas and devised a plan. He transformed himself into a small, harmless creature — sometimes a rabbit, sometimes a mouse — and snuck into Grasshopper's lodge while he was away. He found the tobacco bundled in a pouch and escaped with it. Grasshopper pursued but Gluskabe was too swift. He distributed the tobacco among the Wabanaki tribes, teaching them how to plant and harvest it and how to offer it in sacred pipes. The smoke rising from the pipes carries the people's prayers directly to Gichi Niwaskw, the Great Spirit, and Gluskabe is honored for this gift that connects the people with the divine.

creature.name: Aziza
creature.summary: Aziza are benevolent forest spirits of Fon and Dahomean mythology in Benin, small fairy-like beings who guard the wilderness and grant magical powers to hunters.

story.title: How Glooscap Found the Summer
story.summary: In the long-ago time, there was no summer — only endless winter. The earth was covered in snow and ice, the people were freezing, and the animals suffered. Glooscap decided to find the spirit of summer and bring it back. He traveled to the far north where Winter, a powerful giant, held Summer captive in his ice lodge. Glooscap challenged Winter to a contest of power. They told stories for many days, and as Winter talked, frost grew thicker on the walls. But Glooscap's stories were of warmth, green leaves, and flowing water. He so charmed the spirit of Summer that she awakened and began to melt Winter's ice. Winter retreated north, and Summer followed Glooscap back to the people. Ever since, Summer and Winter alternate — Winter rules for half the year, but when his power wanes, Summer returns and the world thaws. The Mi'kmaq celebrate this cycle as the eternal rhythm of life.

creature.name: Mami Wata
creature.summary: Beautiful light-skinned woman with very long hair, sometimes with fish tail

story.title: Ableegumooch: How Rabbit Lost His Tail
story.summary: Ableegumooch the Rabbit was once the most vain of all animals, boasting constantly about his beautiful long tail. He teased Otter for having only a small, stubby tail. Annoyed, Otter challenged Rabbit to a fishing contest. Rabbit, who knew nothing about fishing but would never admit it, agreed. Otter caught fish after fish by diving into the river, while Rabbit sat on the bank with a line, catching nothing. In desperation, Rabbit tied his line to his tail and cast it far into the water, but instead of catching a fish, a giant turtle grabbed his tail and pulled. Rabbit escaped but his magnificent tail was snapped off, leaving only the short stub rabbits have to this day. Otter laughed at Rabbit's vanity, and Rabbit learned that pride comes before a fall. Glooscap, watching from his lodge, declared that Rabbit's new tail would remind all creatures of the dangers of vanity.

creature.name: Asiman
creature.summary: A flying vampire witch who can transform into various animals and humans

story.title: Gluskabe and the Monster Frog
story.summary: A devastating drought struck the land of the Wabanaki. Rivers dried to dust, the lakes shrank, and the people were dying. A giant frog monster had swallowed all the water and held it captive in its bloated body. The people called to Gluskabe for help. Gluskabe found the giant frog sunning itself on a rock, swollen with all the water of the world. He approached carefully and, using his magic, made the frog laugh. As the frog's great mouth opened, a flood of water poured forth, refilling the rivers and lakes. Some of the animals that had been trapped in the frog's belly leaped out transformed — those who had been four-legged became fish, and those who had been birds became waterfowl. Gluskabe then shrunk the frog down to its present size and declared that from then on, frogs would live near water but never again swallow more than they needed.

creature.name: Zangbeto
creature.summary: Towering raffia night guardians of Togo's Vodun faith that spin through villages protecting communities and dispensing impartial justice

story.title: The Flying Canoe (Passamaquoddy)
story.summary: Three Passamaquoddy brothers, all skilled canoe-builders, competed to see who could build the finest canoe. The eldest two built large, sturdy vessels decorated with porcupine quills and painted designs. But the youngest brother, instead of building an ordinary canoe, consulted the spirits and built a magical canoe that could fly through the air as easily as it could glide across water. When the day of judgment came, the two older brothers mocked the youngest's strange craft. But when the youngest sang a special song, his canoe rose into the air and circled the village. The chief was so impressed that he gave his daughter to the youngest brother in marriage. The story celebrates innovation and the wisdom of seeking spiritual guidance rather than merely following tradition, a theme common to Wabanaki folktales.

creature.name: Mami Wata
creature.summary: Beautiful light-skinned woman with very long hair, sometimes with fish tail

story.title: The Origin of the Thunderbird (Wabanaki)
story.summary: In the Wabanaki tradition, the Thunderbird was once a great chief who loved his people so much that after his death, the Great Spirit transformed him into a giant bird whose wings make the thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He was given dominion over the sky and tasked with hunting the great horned serpent Weewillmekq (Jipijka'm), who lurked in lakes and devoured people. Whenever the horned serpent rose to attack, the Thunderbird descended from the clouds and struck it with lightning. The Thunderbird had a nest on the highest peak of the mountains, and its eggs were made of solid lightning. The Wabanaki honored the Thunderbird with offerings of tobacco, asking it to bring rain for the crops and to protect them from the underworld monsters.

creature.name: Nyonyose Mask Spirit
creature.summary: Ancestral spirits of the Mossi who use animal masks to guide the dead and protect the living

story.title: The Owl Husband (Passamaquoddy)
story.summary: A beautiful young Passamaquoddy woman was visited each night by a mysterious man who came to her lodge after dark. He was kind and gentle, and she grew to love him, though she had never seen his face clearly. Her parents warned her to discover his identity. One night, she placed ashes near the doorway. When the man left, his footprints showed the marks of an owl's claws. The next night, she hid and watched, and saw her husband transform into a great horned owl and fly away. Heartbroken but determined, she followed him into the forest. The owl tried to keep her as his wife in his tree-home, but she longed for her human family. Finally, the owl released her, but she was never the same — she had seen the spirit world and could not fully return to human life. The story teaches that love between different kinds of beings cannot overcome the fundamental boundaries of nature.

creature.name: Tengbiswem Earth Spirit
creature.summary: The invisible guardian of the soil in Mossi culture, controlling fertility and requiring ritual appeasement

story.title: Kanati and Selu: The Origin of Game and Corn (Cherokee)
story.summary: Kanati (The Lucky Hunter) and Selu (Corn) were the first Cherokee man and woman. Kanati would hunt by moving a rock at the entrance of a cave, releasing an animal and killing it. Their son befriended a Wild Boy born from the blood of slaughtered game. The boys secretly followed Kanati and discovered the cave; they opened it, allowing all animals to escape, which is why humans must hunt for food today. Selu would produce corn by rubbing her stomach, and beans by rubbing her sides. When the boys discovered her secret, Selu knew she would die. She instructed them to drag her body seven times around a cleared circle, then seven times inside it, and corn would grow by morning. The boys did not complete the ritual properly, which is why corn only grows in certain places. The story establishes the Cherokee relationship with hunting, agriculture, and the origin of food scarcity.

creature.name: The Tanganyika Serpent
creature.summary: A silver serpent guarding the depths of Lake Tanganyika in Burundi

story.title: The Creation of Earth and the Great Buzzard (Cherokee)
story.summary: In the beginning, all was water, and animals lived in the sky world above the stone vault. The water beetle Dâyuni'sï volunteered to explore below and brought up soft mud from the ocean floor, which grew into the earth. The earth was initially soft and flat. The Great Buzzard flew down to survey the land, and his wings striking the ground created the mountains and valleys of Cherokee territory. When the animals saw what the Buzzard had done, they feared he would make the earth too rough, so they called him back, leaving the Cherokee mountains steep and the valleys deep. The sun was set on a track to travel across the sky each day. This foundational myth explains the geography of the Southern Appalachian region and establishes the Cherokee cosmic order.

creature.name: The Mountain Giant
creature.summary: A colossal stone-skinned giant inhabiting the mountains of Burundi

story.title: Uktena: The Horned Serpent (Cherokee)
story.summary: Uktena is a massive horned serpent covered in shining scales, with a single blazing crystal in its forehead that grants supernatural vision. The first Uktena was once a man who attempted to kill the sun. He failed and was transformed into the monstrous serpent as punishment. Uktena dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and under mountains. Its gaze alone can paralyze or kill. Only the bravest medicine men and heroes dare to hunt Uktena, seeking the Ulûñsû'tî, the diamond-like crystal from its forehead, which grants great power to whoever possesses it. The most famous story involves a hunter who stalked an Uktena to its lair and, after a great battle, retrieved the crystal. The stone brought power but also danger, and was eventually hidden away in a sacred place.

creature.name: The Night-Walker
creature.summary: A spectral night-spirit that feeds on fear and dreams in Burundi

story.title: The Nunnehi: Cherokee Spirit People (Cherokee)
story.summary: The Nunnehi, meaning 'The Travelers' or 'Those Who Live Anywhere,' are a race of invisible spirit people who dwell in the mountains and forests of Cherokee country. They are friendly toward humans and often appear as regal Cherokee warriors. The Nunnehi are said to be great dancers and musicians; travelers sometimes hear their singing and drumming coming from inside hollow mountains. They have saved Cherokee war parties from defeat by magically enlarging their numbers or by confusing enemy forces. The Nunnehi are known to invite favored humans into their underground dwellings, where time passes differently — a visitor may spend what seems like a single night only to return home and find that years have passed. They are generally benevolent but withdraw from contact if treated with disrespect.

creature.name: Kiranga
creature.summary: Kiranga is a Burundian hero-spirit who leads the Imandwa spirit society, possessing mediums to diagnose illnesses and intercede between humans and the divine Imana.

story.title: Yunwi Tsunsdi: The Little People (Cherokee)
story.summary: Yunwi Tsunsdi are the Cherokee Little People — small, child-sized nature spirits who live in caves, under rocks, and in the dense forest. They are usually invisible but sometimes reveal themselves to humans they trust. They possess powerful magic and are said to have taught medicine to certain shamans. The Little People can be helpful to those who respect them, leading lost hunters to safety or granting blessings. However, they are easily angered by disrespect and punish those who bother them excessively with confusion or misfortune. They are known to borrow tools from villagers, always returning them with small gifts of thanks. The Yunwi Tsunsdi are not to be spoken of lightly; those who encounter them rarely discuss the experience directly.

creature.name: Imandwa Spirits
creature.summary: The Imandwa are the forty-spirit pantheon of Burundi's Kubandwa cult, serving as active mediators between humanity and the supreme god Imana in all aspects of life

story.title: Spearfinger (U'tlun'ta): The Stone Witch (Cherokee)
story.summary: Spearfinger, also known as Nûñ'yunu'ï or 'Stone-dress,' is a fearsome Cherokee monster and witch who lives along the eastern side of Tennessee and western North Carolina. She has a long, sharp forefinger on her right hand like a spear or obsidian knife, which she uses to cut open her victims. She wears a dress made of stone that makes her nearly invulnerable. Spearfinger feeds on human livers, especially those of children. Her mouth is perpetually stained with blood. She can mimic the voices of loved ones to lure victims close. According to legend, she was eventually defeated by a group of Cherokee warriors who discovered that her only vulnerable spot was a small point on her palm. They shot arrows into her palm, and she fell from the mountain where she lived.

creature.name: Imana
creature.summary: Imana is the supreme creator god of Burundi and Rwanda, an almighty but remote deity who created the world and delegates daily spiritual mediation to the Imandwa spirits

story.title: Raven Mocker (Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï) (Cherokee)
story.summary: Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï, the Raven Mocker, is a malevolent Cherokee spirit that preys on the dying. These witches are said to be ordinary-looking people during the day who transform at night into raven-like spirits. They gather around the home of a dying person and torment them, stealing their remaining years of life for themselves. The Raven Mocker flies with a sound like rushing wind and can only be seen by medicine men. After a person dies, the Raven Mockers eat the heart of the victim. The only defense against a Raven Mocker is a medicine man who knows the proper rituals to drive them away. Raven Mockers are visible only to medicine men, who can identify them even in their human form by their sleepless, bloodshot eyes and their habit of appearing exhausted from their nighttime flights.

creature.name: Bu Draya
creature.summary: Terrifying sea jinn from Bahraini and Gulf folklore that preys on pearl divers, mimicking drowning cries to lure victims in the Arabian Gulf

story.title: The Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) (Cherokee)
story.summary: The Cherokee believe in the Thunder Beings, known as Aniyvdaqualosgi or Ani-Yuntikwalaski. The Great Thunder and his two sons, the Thunder Boys, live in the land of the west above the sky vault. They dress in lightning and rainbows. Unlike many tribes where thunder spirits take bird form, Cherokee Thunderers are human in form — powerful and dangerous but generally friendly to humans. The priests pray to the Thunder beings for rain and blessings. Some lesser thunder beings live closer to the Earth's surface in cliffs, mountains, and waterfalls, and these are more mischievous, sometimes causing harm. Thunder is said to be the sound of the Great Thunder's wings or his voice rolling across the sky. Lightning is the fire from his eyes.

creature.name: Bou Saadia
creature.summary: Tragic wandering spirit from Tunisian folklore who eternally searches for his lost daughter Saadia, sold into slavery in the Tunis medina

story.title: Grandmother Spider Steals the Fire (Cherokee)
story.summary: In the beginning, the only fire belonged to the Thunders in the sky world. The animals held a council to decide who would bring fire to the people. Many brave animals volunteered but failed: Raven tried to carry an ember but his feathers turned black; Screech Owl's eyes were burned red; Hooting Owl's eyes were singed white. Finally, the tiny Water Spider, Dilsdohdi, volunteered. She spun a bowl-shaped web, placed it on her back, and crossed the water to the sky world. She placed a small ember in her web-basket and carried it safely back across the water to the people. This is why the Water Spider has black downy hair with red stripes — the smoke and fire marked her. Fire became the sacred gift that transformed human life.

creature.name: Basilisk
creature.summary: Legendary serpent king known in Vatican tradition for its lethal gaze, symbolizing the power of sin overcome by Christian faith

story.title: The Origin of Disease and Medicine (Cherokee)
story.summary: Long ago, all plants, animals, and humans lived together in harmony, and animals were larger and stronger. As the human population grew, they began killing animals without respect. The animals held councils to decide how to protect themselves. The Deer council decreed that any hunter who killed a deer without asking forgiveness would develop rheumatism. The Birds, Insects, and smaller animals created diseases to afflict humans. But the Plants heard of the animals' plans. Since plants had always been friends with humans, they vowed that for every disease the animals created, they would provide a cure. This is why every plant has medicinal purpose, and why medicine men must learn from the spirits of plants which herbs to use. The story establishes the Cherokee understanding of balance between humans, animals, and plants.

creature.name: Beaivi
creature.summary: The Sami sun goddess who brings spring, fertility, and mental healing to the Arctic world

story.title: Stone Coat (Nûñ'yunu'ï): The Rock Giants (Cherokee)
story.summary: Stone Coat, also called Nûñ'yunu'ï, is a race of giant beings covered in stone-like skin that makes them nearly invulnerable. They dwell in the remote mountains and caves of Cherokee territory. These rock giants are cannibalistic and prey upon humans who venture too far into their domain. They are incredibly strong, capable of throwing boulders and tearing down trees. Stone Coat is also associated with Spearfinger, who wears a stone dress. The giants' only weakness is their vulnerability to certain spiritual practices. Cherokee medicine men knew rituals to confuse or drive away Stone Coats. The legend may have been inspired by encounters with the fossilized remains of prehistoric megafauna in the Appalachian region, and it serves as a warning against venturing into dangerous, unknown territory.

creature.name: Bieggolmmái
creature.summary: Bieggolmmái is the Sami wind god who controls the winds from his mountain cave using two shovels, essential for safe reindeer herding and travel.

story.title: Tlanuwa: The Giant Raptor (Cherokee)
story.summary: Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey with feathers made of impenetrable metal. This massive raptor could carry off humans and even small deer in its talons. Its feathers were said to be sharp as knives and could be launched as projectiles. The Tlanuwa lived in the highest mountain peaks and remote cliffs. In Cherokee legend, the Tlanuwa sometimes battled the Uktena serpent, their ancient enemy. The birds were also known to fight against humans who invaded their territory. The Tlanuwa appears in stories from many Southeastern tribes including the Creek and Natchez, suggesting it was a widespread figure in the regional mythology. Some accounts describe it as a benevolent protector spirit of the Cherokee people.

creature.name: Tééhoołtsódii (Big Water Creature)
creature.summary: The Navajo creation epic describes four worlds through which the Diyin Dineʼé (Holy People) journeyed.

story.title: The First Strawberries (Cherokee)
story.summary: The first man and the first woman quarreled, and the woman left their home in anger. The man, sad and remorseful, tried to bring her back. The Sun, taking pity on the man, created huckleberries along the path to tempt the woman to stop, but she paid them no mind. Next the Sun created blackberries, but she ignored them too. Finally, the Sun created strawberries — the first ever. When the woman saw the ripe, red berries, she stopped to taste one. The sweetness reminded her of happier times, and she began to gather them. As she looked back down the path, she saw her husband approaching, and she forgave him. They reconciled and returned home together. This Cherokee story explains the origin of strawberries and teaches the power of sweetness and forgiveness in mending relationships.

creature.name: Plat-Eye
creature.summary: The Plat-Eye is a shapeshifting vengeful spirit in Gullah folklore that haunts swamps and graveyards, attacking those who trespass on its territory.

story.title: The Dragon of Lopburi
story.summary: In the ancient city of Lopburi, there lived a powerful dragon beneath the great temple.

creature.name: Pemba
creature.summary: Bambara primordial grain-spirit whose premature creation introduced chaos, representing unbalanced masculine creativity

story.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
story.summary: Anansi tricks humans into giving him all the world's wisdom—but discovers it cannot be kept.

creature.name: Prester John
creature.summary: Prester John was the legendary Christian priest-king of a fabulous eastern kingdom, later identified with the Ethiopian emperor, sought by European explorers for centuries.

story.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
story.summary: In the sun-baked valleys where the dusty trails wound between olive groves and dry riverbeds, the animals of the district had gathered for their usual morning disputes.

creature.name: Pepo (Sea Spirits)
creature.summary: Pepo are powerful sea spirits of the Swahili coast who can possess humans and control destinies, honored through kipemba ceremonies.

story.title: Aladdin and the Magic Lamp
story.summary: In a far city of China, though the tale itself comes from the sands of Arabia, there lived a poor tailor named Mustapha and his wife, who had one son.

creature.name: Pepo wa Bahari (Lord of the Sea)
creature.summary: Pepo wa Bahari is the Lord of the Sea in Swahili mythology, controlling the Indian Ocean's monsoon winds, fish, and storms.

story.title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
story.summary: In a town in Persia, there once lived two brothers.. The elder, Cassim, married a wealthy woman and became the richest merchant in the marketplace.

creature.name: Pate Serpent
creature.summary: The Pate Serpent is a legendary guardian of Pate Island in the Lamu Archipelago, an enormous serpent sung to sleep by Liongo Fumo.

story.title: Scheherazade
story.summary: The chronicles of the Sassanian kings tell of a monarch named Shahryar, who ruled an empire stretching from India to China.
